**Surah "Alam Nashrah" (Ash-Sharh)** is Meccan according to the consensus. It has eight verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ (1)

*Sharh al-sadr* (expansion of the breast) means opening it, that is, "Did We not open your breast to Islam?" Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Did We not soften your heart?" Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They said, "O Messenger of God, does the breast expand?" He said: "Yes, and it becomes spacious." They said, "O Messenger of God, is there a sign of that?" He said: "Yes: turning away from the abode of delusion, turning back to the abode of eternity, and preparing for death before death arrives." This meaning has already passed in *al-Zumar* [[See vol. 15, p. 247]] at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one whose breast God has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord...?﴾ It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said, concerning ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾: "It was filled with wisdom and knowledge."

In the *Sahih* [[This is the narration of al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Tafsir.]] from Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, a man of his people, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was by the House, between sleeping and waking, I heard someone saying: 'One of the three [[In Sahih Muslim it reads "one of the three between the two men." It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was then sleeping with his paternal uncle Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and his cousin Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. See the explanation of this hadith in Sahih Muslim (chapter on the Night Journey). Also in al-Qastallani's commentary, in the Book of the Beginning of Creation (chapter on the mention of the angels).]]...' Then a basin of gold was brought to me, containing Zamzam water, and my breast was expanded down to such-and-such." Qatadah said: "I asked, 'What does that mean?'" He said: "To the bottom of my belly." He said: "Then my heart was extracted, washed with Zamzam water, then returned to its place, and then filled with faith and wisdom." There is a longer account in this hadith.

It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Two angels came to me in the form of a bird, carrying water and snow. One of them expanded my breast, and the other opened it with his beak and washed it therein." In another hadith he said: "An angel came to me, split open my heart, extracted from it a clot, and said: 'Your heart is *wakī'*, your two eyes are seeing, your two ears are hearing. You are Muhammad, the Messenger of God. Your tongue is truthful, your soul is at peace, your character is *qutham*, and you are a guardian [*qayyim*].'"

The lexicographers said: His saying *wakī'* means that it retains what is placed in it. It is said: "a *siqa'* (water-skin) that is *wakī'*," meaning strong, retaining what is put into it. And "his stomach became *istawka'at*," meaning it became strong. His saying *qutham* means comprehensive. It is said: "a man who is *qathum* for good," meaning one who gathers it.

The meaning of ﴿Did We not expand?﴾ is "We have expanded." The evidence for this is His saying that follows it: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾. This is a conjunction according to the *ta'wil* (interpretive meaning), not according to the *tanzil* (literal wording), because if it were according to the *tanzil* He would have said "And We remove from you your burden." This shows that the meaning of ﴿Did We not expand?﴾ is "We have expanded."

*Lam* here is a negation particle (*lam* [لَمْ]). The interrogative (*istifham*, question form) contains an element of negation, and when a negation occurs it returns to affirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin: 8], meaning "God is the most just of judges." Likewise ﴿Is not God sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 36]. Similar to this is the verse of Jarir praising Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

*"Are you not the best of those who have ridden the mounts,*
*and the most generous of all the peoples in the bellies of the wine-jars?"*

The meaning is: "You are such-and-such."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 94, verses 2–3:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾, meaning, We lightened from you your sin. Anas read: "We unloaded and We lowered." Ibn Mas'ud read: "We unloaded from you your load." This verse is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your sin of the past and the future﴾ [al-Fath: 2].[[Verse 2 of surah al-Fath.]] It has been said that all of this was before prophethood (nubuwwah, the office of prophecy). The word wizr means sin. That is, We removed from you what you were engaged in of the affairs of the jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), because he (ﷺ) was in many of the practices of his people, although he had not worshipped an idol or a statue. Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: the Prophet (ﷺ) had sins that weighed heavily upon him, and Allah forgave them for him. ﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾, meaning, it burdened him until he heard its naqid, that is, its sound. The lexicographers say: anqada al-himl zahr al-naqah (the load broke the back of the she-camel) means when you hear from it a creaking from the intensity of the load. Likewise, you hear the naqid of the saddle, that is, its creaking. Jamil said:

*"Until its ropes were pulled taut with a groaning, and the chest-bones of its breast were about to break."*

Bawani zawrihi means the roots of its chest. So the wizr is a heavy load. Al-Muhasibi said: it means the heaviness of the burden had Allah not pardoned it.

﴿Which had weighed down your back﴾, meaning, it made it heavy and weakened it. He said: the sins of the prophets are described with this heaviness, although they are forgiven, because of the intensity of their concern over them, their regret for them, and their grief over them. Al-Suddi said: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾, meaning, We lowered from you your weight. It is in the reading of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "We lowered[[In the Shadhdh of Ibn Khalawayh: "(And We lowered your burden) from Anas ibn Malik." And "(We unloaded and We lowered) both from him and from Ibn Mas'ud."]] from you your load." It has also been said: meaning, We lowered from you the weight of the sins of the jahiliyyah. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it means the mistake and the forgetfulness. It has also been said: it means the sins of your community, which Allah attributed to him because his heart was occupied with them. Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya and Abu Ubaydah said: We lightened from you the burdens of prophethood and its duties, so that they would not weigh upon you. It has also been said: at the beginning, the revelation was heavy upon him, to the point that he almost threw himself from the peak of a mountain, until Jibril came to him and showed him himself, and what he feared of a change in his intellect was removed from him. It has also been said: We protected you from bearing the burden, and We guarded you before prophethood during the forty years from impurities, until revelation came down to you while you were purified of impurities.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 94, verses 5–6:**

﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ (5) ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ (6). That is, indeed with distress and hardship there is ease, meaning ample provision and wealth. Then He repeated it, saying: ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾. Some scholars said: this repetition is for emphasis of the speech, as it is said: "Shoot, shoot!" and "Hurry, hurry!" Allah the Exalted said: ﴿No! You are going to know﴾ [[Verse 3 of Surah Alhakum (al-Takathur).]] ﴿Then, no! You are going to know﴾ (al-Takathur: 3–4). A similar case of repetition in answers is: "Yes, yes," and "No, no." This is for elaboration and emphasis, as said by al-Farra'. From this is the poet's verse:

"I resolved to set my soul against some of the cares,
so woe to my soul, woe to it!" [[The verse is by al-Khansa'. It is also narrated as:
"I resolved to set my soul against all the cares."]]

Some scholars said: it is among the habits of the Arabs that when they mention an indefinite noun and then repeat it, the second is the same as the first, but when they mention it as a definite noun and then repeat it, the second is other than the first. Here the two are distinct, so that the hope is stronger and the call to patience more compelling. This was said by Tha'lab. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah the Exalted says, "I created one hardship, and I created two eases, and one hardship will never overcome two eases." It has come in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this surah that he said: [No hardship will overcome two eases.] Ibn Mas'ud said [that is, in his narration from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)]: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if hardship were inside a stone, ease would seek it until it entered upon it, and one hardship will never overcome two eases." Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah wrote to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab mentioning to him large gatherings of the Romans and what he feared from them. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote back to him: "To proceed: whatever situation of hardship befalls a believing servant, Allah will bring relief after it, and indeed one hardship will never overcome two eases. Allah the Exalted says in His Book: ﴿O you who believe, be patient, endure together, stand ready, and fear Allah that you may be successful﴾ (Al 'Imran: 200). [[Verse of Surah Al 'Imran.]]" [Al 'Imran: 189].

Some scholars, among them al-Jurjani, said: this view is flawed, because according to this gradual reading, if a man says, "With the horseman is a sword, with the horseman is a sword," it would have to follow that there is one horseman and two swords. The correct view is that Allah sent His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) poor and humble, and the polytheists reproached him for his poverty, to the point that they said to him, "We will gather wealth for you." He was grieved and thought that they denied him because of his poverty. So Allah consoled him, enumerated His favours upon him, and promised him wealth by saying: ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, meaning: let not what they reproached you with of poverty grieve you, for with that hardship there is ease that comes quickly, that is, in this world. So Allah fulfilled what He had promised him. He did not die until He had opened the Hijaz and Yemen to him, and widened his means, to the point that he would give a man two hundred camels, bestow generous gifts, and set aside a year's provision for his family. All this favour is of worldly affairs, and although it was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), some of his community may enter into it, if Allah the Exalted wills. Then He began another favour from the Hereafter, which contains consolation and comfort for him (ﷺ). So He began, saying: ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, which is another matter. The evidence that it is a new beginning is that it is not connected by a fa' (then), a waw (and), or any other conjunctive particle that indicates coordination. This is a general promise to all believers, none of whom is excluded from it: that with hardship in this world there is ease in the Hereafter for the believers, without doubt. The ease of this world and the ease of the Hereafter may sometimes be combined. As for what is in the report, [one hardship will never overcome two eases], it means that one hardship will never overcome both of them. It may only overcome one of them, if it overcomes at all, and that is the ease of this world. As for the ease of the Hereafter, it is certain to occur and nothing can overpower it. Or it may be said: with the hardship, namely the expulsion of the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah by its people, there is ease, namely his entry into it on the day of the conquest of Makkah with ten thousand men, with honour and dignity.

**Issue one:** Concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you are free﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: "So when you have finished your prayer, ﴿then labour﴾, that is, strive earnestly in supplication and ask Him for your need." Ibn Mas'ud said: "When you have finished the obligatory duties, ﴿then labour﴾ in the night prayer." Al-Kalbi said: "When you have finished conveying the message, ﴿then labour﴾, that is, seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women." Al-Hasan and Qatadah also said: "When you have finished fighting your enemy, ﴿then labour﴾ in the worship of your Lord." It is related from Mujahid: "When you have finished with your worldly affairs, ﴿then labour﴾ in your prayer," and similarly from al-Hasan. Al-Junayd said: "When you have finished with the affairs of creation, strive diligently in the worship of the Truth."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Among the innovators (al-mubtada'ah) are those who recite this verse as (fa-anṣib), with a kasrah on the ṣād and a hamzah at its beginning [[That is, the hamzat al-wasl (the hamzah of connection), not the hamzat al-qat' (the hamzah of cutting), because its past tense is triliteral: (naṣaba yansibu).]], and they say its meaning is: 'Appoint the imam whom you will make your successor.' This is false in the recitation and false in the meaning, because the Prophet ﷺ did not appoint anyone as successor." Some ignorant people recited it as (fa-anṣabba), with a shaddah on the bā', meaning: "When you have finished the jihad, then hasten to return to your city." This is also false as a recitation, since it contradicts the consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars), but its meaning is sound, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: [Travel is a piece of punishment; it prevents one of you from his sleep, his food and his drink. So when one of you has accomplished his purpose, let him hasten back to his family.] The people most severely punished and most wretched in their return and destination are those who take a sound meaning and then construct upon it, from their own opinion, a recitation or a hadith; such a person is lying against Allah and against His Messenger, and who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?

Al-Mahdawi said: It is related from Abu Ja'far al-Mansur that he recited (a-lam nashraḥ laka ṣadraka) with a fatḥah on the ḥā', and this is far-fetched. It may be interpreted by supposing the light nun (nūn al-khafīfah), which at pause was changed into an alif, then the continuous recitation (wasl) was made to follow the pausal form (waqf), and then the alif was deleted. He cited as evidence:

*"Strike away from yourself the cares that come by night, / striking as you strike the horse's forehead with the whip."*

He meant: (iḍribanna), with the emphatic nun.

It is related from Abu al-Simal (fa-idhā fariḡta) with a kasrah on the rā', and this is a dialectal form of it. It is also recited (fa-raghghib), meaning: "Make people desire what is with Him."

**Issue two:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: It is related from Shurayh that he passed by people playing on a day of 'Eid, and he said: "The Lawgiver did not command this." But this is open to question, for the Abyssinians used to play with shields and spears in the mosque on the day of 'Eid while the Prophet ﷺ watched. Abu Bakr entered the house of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, where 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was, and with her were two young girls from the young women of the Ansar singing. Abu Bakr said: "The flute of Satan in the house of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said: [Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for it is a day of 'Eid.] It does not follow that constant exertion in work is required; rather, it is disliked by creation.
